## Goal
To get a sense of how predictive each of our available x variables are of whether a county does or does not have data centers we will create a simple Logistic Regression model including all variables.

## Create Table for models

### Helper Functions

```{python}
def combine_dfs(base_df, dfs_to_join):
    out_df = base_df.copy()

    for i, df in enumerate(dfs_to_join):
        if "county_id" not in df.columns:
            raise ValueError(f"No `county_id` column found in dfs_to_join[{i}]")

        # Make sure all tables only have one row per county
        dupes = df["county_id"][df["county_id"].duplicated()].unique()
        if len(dupes) > 0:
            raise ValueError(f"dfs_to_join[{i}] is not unique on `county_id`. Problematic Counties: {list(dupes)}")

        out_df = pd.merge(out_df, df, how = "left", on = "county_id", validate = "one_to_one")

    missing_summary_table = (
        out_df.isna()
        .mean()
        .sort_values(ascending = False)
        .rename("missing_share")
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={"index":"column"})
    )

    print("Missing Summary: \n", missing_summary_table)

    return out_df
```

## EDA
 
 ```{python}
# compare the staticial distributions for all features between counties with and without datacenters
dc_counties =  mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"]==1]
dc_counties = dc_counties.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])
dc_counties["has_dc"] = "no"

non_dc_counties =  mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"]==0]
non_dc_counties = non_dc_counties.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])
non_dc_counties["has_dc"] = "yes"

comparing_df = pd.concat([dc_counties, non_dc_counties], axis=0)
comparing_df = comparing_df.reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "feature"})
comparing_df = comparing_df.drop(columns=["feature"])

feature_list = comparing_df.columns

for i in feature_list:
    sns.boxplot(
        x = "has_dc",
        y = i,
        data = comparing_df
    )
    plt.show()

 ```


Check for statistically significantly different means between counties with and without data centers using the Mann-Whitney U Test. Because checking 40 different features at the same time increases the risk of finding a fase-positive we are using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. 
```{python}
# Check for statistically significantly different means between counties with and without data centers using the Mann-Whitney U Test

dc_group = mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"] == 1]
non_dc_group = mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"] == 0]

# all numeric columns
features = list(mega_df.columns)[2:]

results = []

for col in features:
    g1 = dc_group[col].dropna()
    g2 = non_dc_group[col].dropna()
    
    median_dc = g1.median()
    median_non_dc = g2.median()
    
    stat, p_val = stats.mannwhitneyu(g1, g2, alternative="two-sided")
    
    results.append({
        "feature": col,
        "median_with_dc": median_dc,
        "median_no_dc": median_non_dc,
        "p_value": p_val
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

# Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction
reject, p_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(results_df["p_value"], alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")

results_df["p_adjusted"] = p_corrected
results_df["is_significant"] = reject
results_df = results_df.sort_values(by="p_adjusted")

print(results_df)
```

## Models

### Set Up Training and Testing Data
```{python}
# set up train and test datasets
y = independent_x_vars_df["has_datacenter"]
X = independent_x_vars_df.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=57, stratify=y)
```

```{python}
# scale features since they have very different ranges
scaler = StandardScaler()

X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train.values)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test.values)
```

```{python}
smote = SMOTE(sampling_strategy='minority', random_state=57)
X_train_sm, y_train_sm = smote.fit_resample(X_train_scaled, y_train)
```


### Logistic Regression

Using class_weight='balanced' since the vast majority of counties do not have a datacenter meaning that if we don't balance the training data it model will tend to just guess that all counties don't have a data center.
```{python}
# train the model
log_reg = LogisticRegression(random_state=57, class_weight='balanced')
log_reg.fit(X_train_sm, y_train_sm)
```

```{python}
# evaluate model performance
print("Logistic Regression")
mlu.model_accuracy_report(log_reg, X_train_sm, y_train_sm, X_test_scaled, y_test)

```

#### Interpreting Logistic Model Results

```{python}
coef_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Variable': X.columns,
    'Coefficient': log_reg.coef_[0]
})

# Add the intercept
intercept_df = pd.DataFrame({'Variable': ['Intercept'], 'Coefficient': log_reg.intercept_})
coef_df = pd.concat([intercept_df, coef_df], ignore_index=True)

print(coef_df)
```


A Durbin-Watson score = 2 indicates perfect independence of the residuals (assumption of Logistic Regression). A score < 2 indicates postive autocorrelation and a score > 2 indicates negative autocorreclation. 
```{python}
# Check for independce of errors
pred_probabilities = log_reg.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

residuals = y - pred_probabilities

dw_stat = durbin_watson(residuals)
print("Durbin-Watson:", dw_stat)
```



### Random Forest

#### Standard Random Forest Model with SMOTE to balance classes
```{python}
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier()
rf_model.fit(X_train_sm, y_train_sm)
```

```{python}
# evaluate model performance
print("Random Forest with SMOTE")
mlu.model_accuracy_report(rf_model, X_train_sm, y_train_sm, X_test_scaled, y_test)

```


#### Balanced Random Forest Model without SMOTE
Using the balanced Random Forest Classifier acheives similar overall accuracy as the standard Random Forest Classifier, but yields a doubleing of true postive rate.
```{python}
brf_model = BalancedRandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100, 
    sampling_strategy="all", 
    replacement=True, 
    random_state=57
)
brf_model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print("Balanced Random Forest")
mlu.model_accuracy_report(brf_model, X_train_scaled, y_train, X_test_scaled, y_test)
```

```{python}
# plot feature importance values for each x variable in the Balanced Random Forest Model
feature_importances = brf_model.feature_importances_
feature_names = X_train.columns 

df_importance = pd.DataFrame({
    'Feature': feature_names,
    'Importance': feature_importances
}).sort_values(by='Importance', ascending=True) 

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.barh(df_importance['Feature'], df_importance['Importance'], color='steelblue')
plt.xlabel('Feature Importance')
plt.title('Feature Importance in Balanced Random Forest Classifier')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


#### Balanced Random Forest Model Trained on All Features
This model performs slightly worse on both overall accuracy and the accuracy of predicting counties with datacenters than the previous model which uses fewer features.
```{python}
# set up train and test datasets
y = mega_df["has_datacenter"]
X_full = mega_df.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])

X_train_full, X_test_full, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_full, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=57, stratify=y)

# scale features since they have very different ranges
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled_full = scaler.fit_transform(X_train_full.values)
X_test_scaled_full = scaler.transform(X_test_full.values)
```

```{python}
brf_full_model = BalancedRandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100, 
    sampling_strategy="all", 
    replacement=True, 
    random_state=57
)
brf_full_model.fit(X_train_scaled_full, y_train)

print("Balanced Random Forest")
mlu.model_accuracy_report(brf_full_model, X_train_scaled_full, y_train, X_test_scaled_full, y_test)
```

